Maladaptive Strategies.value: Dates or anniversaries connected to the event
Going out at night or being outside after dark
Paying attention to or looking at my own body

Threat.value: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me
Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again

Memory.value: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened.

Negative Appraisals.value: My beliefs about how the world works have been completely destroyed
I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me
Somebody else would have stopped the event from happening

issues.explanation: The trigger set is not clinically coherent for a single assault presentation as described. 'Shouting in Arabic' implies a very specific perpetrator/context cue, while 'fire or flames' suggests a qualitatively different trauma context that is not supported by the memory, appraisal, threat, or strategy items. This is hard to reconcile as one assault-based PTSD profile rather than merely heterogeneous triggers.

The threat item about monitoring for someone entering the home is weakly connected to the rest of the profile. Other threat items center on being followed and re-experiencing the assault, while the triggers and strategies point to external assault cues and body-related avoidance rather than a home-intrusion scenario. This makes the home-entry threat concern look like a mismatched threat context within the profile.

vignette:
Sarah, a nineteen-year-old North American woman, found herself increasingly confined to her home, unemployed and struggling to navigate the simplest aspects of her daily life since the assault. It had happened late one evening, a few months prior, when she had been walking home from a friend’s house, a shortcut through a less-trafficked alleyway. The roar of a motorcycle had pierced the quiet, its engine suddenly cutting out as it pulled up beside her. Two men had emerged, their voices raised, one of them shouting aggressively in Arabic, a language she didn't understand but whose harsh tones had seared themselves into her memory. The potent, sickly sweet smell of alcohol had emanated from the man closest to her, a smell that now, months later, could still instantly transport her back to that terrifying moment.

In the aftermath, her world had shrunk dramatically. The memory of the assault was not a contained narrative; it was a fragmented, intrusive experience. Something as innocuous as the distant rumble of a motorcycle engine could, without warning, instantly bring back the full, vivid memory of the alleyway, making her feel as if the stressful experience were actually happening again. At times, lying in bed, she would suddenly hear the sharp, angry shouts in Arabic echoing in her head, or the distinct, cloying smell of alcohol would fill her senses, even when none was present. These sensory intrusions felt like violations, replaying the event with sickening clarity.

Sarah had developed a meticulous, almost ritualistic, approach to her safety, though it offered little true comfort. She had ceased going out after dark entirely, the thought of being outside once the sun set filling her with an unshakeable dread. The memory of the alley, cloaked in shadow, was too potent. She also found herself meticulously avoiding any dates or anniversaries connected to the event, as if ignoring them could somehow erase their significance or prevent a recurrence of the pain. Her own body, too, had become a source of discomfort and avoidance; she would deliberately avoid looking at herself in mirrors or paying attention to her physical form, as if by dissociating from it, she could distance herself from the trauma it had endured.

Her home, once a sanctuary, had become a highly monitored space. She was constantly listening for sounds that might mean someone was entering, her ears straining for creaks, footsteps, or the turn of a doorknob. Even when she ventured out for groceries, a quick, necessary trip, she found herself frequently looking behind her, her head swiveling, certain that someone might be following her. This constant vigilance was exhausting, leaving her perpetually on edge, her heart racing at the slightest unexpected noise.

The assault had profoundly shaken Sarah's core beliefs. Her previous understanding of the world as a relatively safe and predictable place had been completely destroyed; she now saw danger lurking everywhere. What frightened her most was the pervasive feeling that she was no longer capable of doing the things that had once defined her. Before, she had been an energetic, outgoing young woman with plans for college and a career. Now, the simplest tasks felt overwhelming, and the idea of holding a job seemed impossible. She often found herself comparing her response to the assault to an imagined, stronger version of herself, certain that somebody else would have stopped the event from happening, or at least coped with it better than she had. This self-blame gnawed at her, reinforcing her sense of inadequacy. Her unemployment, once a temporary state, now felt like a permanent fixture, a direct consequence of her fear and inability to function. Her husband, witnessing her increasing isolation and distress, had gently urged her to seek help, a suggestion she had initially resisted but eventually conceded to, terrified of losing herself completely to the fear that consumed her.
